title: Root-monomial maps and scheme-theoretic kernel coordinates
statement:
Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], of characteristic exponent $p$ ($p=1$ in characteristic zero). Let $(G_1,T_1)$ and $(G_0,T_0)$ be split reductive affine $F$-group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] with reduced root data $(M_i,\Phi_i,M_i^\vee,\Phi_i^\vee)$ as in [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure], and root groups as in [lem-sfb-reductive-root-subgroup-parametrizations]. Suppose a homomorphism $f:G_1\to G_0$ is already given, with $f(T_1)\subseteq T_0$. Write $u=(f|_{T_1})^*:M_0\to M_1$. Assume $u$ is injective with finite cokernel, and there are a bijection $b:\Phi_1\to\Phi_0$ and $q_\alpha\in\{p^e:e\geq0\}$ such that
$$u(b(\alpha))=q_\alpha\alpha,\qquad u^\vee(\alpha^\vee)=q_\alpha b(\alpha)^\vee.$$
Then $f$ is surjective and faithfully flat and has finite scheme-theoretic kernel $K$; faithfully flat means that extension of scalars along $F[G_0]\to F[G_1]$ is exact and detects zero modules, and finite means finite-dimensional coordinate algebra. For arbitrary root parametrizations $x_{i,\gamma}:\mathbf G_a\xrightarrow{\sim}U_{i,\gamma}$ there are $c_\alpha\in F^\times$ such that
$$f(x_{1,\alpha}(a))=x_{0,b(\alpha)}(c_\alpha a^{q_\alpha})$$
for every commutative $F$-algebra $A$ and $a\in A$. Let $\Phi_1^+$ be any positive-root system and order its positive and negative roots. The multiplication map
$$\left(\prod_{\alpha\in-\Phi_1^+}U_{1,\alpha}\right)\times_FT_1\times_F\left(\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi_1^+}U_{1,\alpha}\right)\longrightarrow G_1$$
is an isomorphism onto a dense open subscheme $C_1$ containing $K$. Under these multiplication coordinates it restricts to an isomorphism of $F$-schemes
$$\left(\prod_{\alpha\in-\Phi_1^+}\mathcal A_{q_\alpha}\right)\times_F\ker(f|_{T_1})\times_F\left(\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi_1^+}\mathcal A_{q_\alpha}\right)\xrightarrow{\sim}K,$$
where $\mathcal A_q=\operatorname{Spec}F[z]/(z^q)$ is embedded into $U_{1,\alpha}$ by $x_{1,\alpha}$. This is an isomorphism of schemes, with no assertion that multiplication identifies the displayed product group law with that on $K$. Moreover $T_1\cap U_{1,\alpha}$ is the trivial subgroup scheme for every $\alpha$. Empty root sets and $q=1$ are allowed, in which case the corresponding $\mathcal A_1$ factor is the trivial scheme. No smoothness or reducedness of $K$ is assumed.

source.place: Lemma 23.10, printed p.487 (recognition of an existing homomorphism as an isogeny); proof of Proposition 23.5, pp.485--486, formulas (144)--(147); Theorem 21.84 and Summary 21.86, p.451 (big-cell multiplication coordinates). The kernel-coordinate statement spells out the fibre over the identity in those coordinates, retaining the Frobenius kernels; all closed kernel points lie in the torus because a finite normal reduced subgroup of a connected group is central. Faithful flatness is the quotient-map property of surjective homomorphisms, Proposition 5.43, p.107.

proof.text: Put $h=f|_{T_1}$. Character antiduality identifies $T_i$ with $D_F(M_i)$ and $h^*:F[M_0]\to F[M_1]$ with $e_m\mapsto e_{u(m)}$. Representatives for the finite group $M_1/u(M_0)$ give a free basis over $F[M_0]$, of positive finite rank. Hence $h^*$ is faithfully flat. Its identity fibre is $H=\ker h=D_F(M_1/u(M_0))$, because quotienting by $e_{u(m)}-1$ identifies precisely the exponents in the same coset. Thus $F[H]$ is finite-dimensional. The finite-index lattice inclusion also gives $M_{0,\mathbf Q}\simeq M_{1,\mathbf Q}$.

source.place: Lemma 23.10, p.487, torus restriction; group-algebra calculation as in Chapter 12.

proof.text: We first obtain big-cell coordinates without assuming anything about $f$. Fix any positive system $\Psi^+$ for a pair $(G,T)$. A rational functional strictly positive on its simple roots extends to $M_{\mathbf Q}$; multiply by a common denominator to obtain a regular cocharacter $\lambda$. The regular-cocharacter theorem gives $B=P(\lambda)$ with positive roots $\Psi^+$. Let $V=R_u(B)$ and take the longest Weyl element and a representative $n_0$ from the Bruhat-chart node. Left translation by $n_0^{-1}$ carries its open dense cell $Vn_0B$ to $(n_0^{-1}Vn_0)B$. Conjugation by $n_0^{-1}$ carries $U_\gamma$ onto $U_{w_0\gamma}$: its tangent space has that character and the uniqueness clause of the root-subgroup node applies. The root-product theorem in any enumeration therefore identifies $n_0^{-1}Vn_0$ with the ordered negative-root product. Combine the ordered positive-root product with $B=V\rtimes T$: the change $(v,t)\mapsto(t,t^{-1}vt)$ gives $B\simeq T\times V$ by multiplication. We obtain an isomorphism $U^-\times T\times U^+\simeq C\subset G$, open dense and containing $1$. It is $T$-equivariant for conjugation, since every factor is normalized by $T$. Both $G$ and its cell are integral by the Bruhat-chart node. In these coordinates $T$ and each root factor meet only at $1$ on every test algebra, proving already $T\cap U_\gamma=1$ as schemes.

source.place: Theorem 21.84 and Summary 21.86, p.451; the translated longest cell is the displayed multiplication chart.

proof.text: Fix $\alpha\in\Phi_1$ and set $y=f\circ x_{1,\alpha}:\mathbf A^1\to G_0$. The conjugation formula gives $y(\alpha(t)a)=h(t)y(a)h(t)^{-1}$ as morphisms. The inverse image $W=y^{-1}(C_0)$ of the cell of step 2 is open, contains $0$, and is invariant under scaling by $\alpha(T_1(F))=F^\times$. The latter equality follows directly by writing the nonzero character $\alpha$ as an integer monomial in split-torus coordinates and taking roots in $F$. If the closed complement contained a nonzero $F$-point, scaling would put every nonzero $F$-point in it; a polynomial vanishing at all such points is zero since $F$ is infinite, forcing the complement to contain $0$. This is impossible. Every point of $\operatorname{Spec}F[a]$ is either the generic point or an $F$-point; the generic point belongs to the nonempty open $W$. Thus $W=\mathbf A^1$, and $y$ factors through $C_0$ as a scheme morphism.

source.place: Proof of Proposition 23.5, pp.485--486, (144)--(147); direct equivariant big-cell argument supplies the root-image assertion used in Lemma 23.10.

proof.text: In the coordinates of $C_0$, the torus component of $y$ is constantly $1$: its characters are units of $F[a]$, hence constants, and $y(0)=1$. For each root $\beta$ the root coordinate is a polynomial $P_\beta(a)$ with zero constant term. Equivariance in the universal ring $F[M_1][a]$ gives $P_\beta(\alpha(t)a)=u(\beta)(t)P_\beta(a)$. A nonzero coefficient of $a^n$ therefore requires $n\alpha=u(\beta)$, since the group-algebra characters are linearly independent. Write $\beta=b(\gamma)$ and use $u(\beta)=q_\gamma\gamma$. Reducedness implies that a positive rational multiple of a root is another root only on the same positive ray: hence $\gamma=\alpha$ and $n=q_\alpha$. Consequently all other coordinates vanish and $f(x_{1,\alpha}(a))=x_{0,b(\alpha)}(c_\alpha a^{q_\alpha})$ for some $c_\alpha\in F$, possibly zero at this point. This is a polynomial identity, so holds over every commutative test algebra.

source.place: Proposition 23.5, formulas (146)--(147), pp.485--486; coefficient comparison before asserting nonvanishing.

proof.text: In fact $c_\alpha\ne0$. Otherwise $f$ kills $U_{1,\alpha}$. Apply the rank-one node to obtain $v_\alpha:\operatorname{SL}_2\to G_{1,\alpha}\subseteq G_1$, identifying the upper unitriangular subgroup with $U_{1,\alpha}$ and the diagonal with $\alpha^\vee$. Then $f v_\alpha$ kills upper unitriangular matrices, and also lower ones since these are conjugates by $w(1)$ defined below. Write $e_+(s)=I+sE_{12}$ and $e_-(s)=I+sE_{21}$, where $E_{ij}$ is the matrix unit, and put $w(s)=e_+(s)e_-(-s^{-1})e_+(s)$. Direct multiplication gives $w(s)w(-1)=\operatorname{diag}(s,s^{-1})$. Thus $h\alpha^\vee(s)=1$ for every $s\in F^\times$. Evaluating the character $b(\alpha)$ instead gives $b(\alpha)(h\alpha^\vee(s))=s^{\langle q_\alpha\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle}=s^{2q_\alpha}$, which is not constantly $1$ on the infinite field $F$. Contradiction, including in characteristic two. The rank-one theorem is applied only to the given reductive group and its root, not to $f$ as an already known isogeny.

source.place: Lemma 23.10, p.487, nontriviality implicit in “as in the proof of Proposition 23.5”; explicit rank-one verification using Theorem 21.11.

proof.text: The positive systems correspond. Indeed a regular rational functional defining $\Phi_1^+$ transports along $u_{\mathbf Q}$ to one whose value at $b(\alpha)$ is $q_\alpha$ times its value at $\alpha$, so the positive roots in $G_0$ are exactly $b(\Phi_1^+)$. Choose the corresponding cell $C_0$ and use on each sign its root enumeration induced by the chosen enumeration for $G_1$. Also $b(-\alpha)=-b(\alpha)$ and $q_{-\alpha}=q_\alpha$: apply $u_{\mathbf Q}^{-1}$ and use reducedness on the opposite ray. Since $f$ is a homomorphism, steps 1 and 4--5 identify $f|_{C_1}:C_1\to C_0$ with the product of $h$ and the maps $a\mapsto c_\alpha a^{q_\alpha}$, in the same multiplication order. Each polynomial map induces a finite free positive-rank extension with basis $1,a,\ldots,a^{q_\alpha-1}$; tensoring these bases with the coset basis in step 1 proves that this product map is finite free and faithfully flat.

Factor $f=j\circ v:G_1\to I\hookrightarrow G_0$ by the affine faithfully-flat image theorem, so $v$ is faithfully flat on coordinate algebras. Let $J\subset F[G_0]$ define $I$. Its restriction to $C_0$ pulls back to zero on $C_1$. But $\mathcal O(C_0)\to\mathcal O(C_1)$ is injective by the free basis of step 6, so $J$ restricts to zero on $C_0$. The restriction $F[G_0]\to\mathcal O(C_0)$ is injective because $G_0$ is integral and $C_0$ is dense open. Therefore $J=0$, $I=G_0$, and $f$ is faithfully flat in the precise module sense in the statement. The faithfully-flat spectrum theorem then makes $f$ surjective on schemes.

source.place: Lemma 23.10, p.487; affine homomorphism theorem 3.34, p.75; Proposition 5.43, p.109 (correcting the inherited page 107).

proof.text: Before asserting that the whole kernel lies in $C_1$, compute its open part $V=K\cap C_1$. As $1\in C_0$, it is exactly the identity fibre of the product map in step 6. On every test algebra the equations are $h(t)=1$ and $c_\alpha a_\alpha^{q_\alpha}=0$ independently for each root coordinate. Since $c_\alpha$ is a unit, these are $a_\alpha^{q_\alpha}=0$. Thus multiplication identifies $V$ as a scheme with the displayed ordered product of $\mathcal A_{q_\alpha}$ and $H=\ker h$. Its coordinate algebra is a tensor product of $F[H]$ and the finite-dimensional rings $F[a_\alpha]/(a_\alpha^{q_\alpha})$, and so is finite-dimensional. This computation makes no assertion about a product group law.

source.place: Theorem 21.84, p.451, identity fibre combined with formula (145), p.485; explicit fibre calculation.

proof.text: The kernel is a closed normal finite-type subgroup by the group-homomorphism factorization node; in particular it is affine. For every $k\in K(F)$, left translation carries the finite open neighbourhood $V$ of $1$ onto a finite open neighbourhood $kV$ of $k$ in $K$. Every closed point of $K$ is an $F$-point by the closed-point residue-field theorem. The union of these opens therefore has empty closed complement: otherwise the Jacobson density theorem would give a closed point in that complement. They cover $K$, and quasi-compactness of the affine scheme $K$ supplies finitely many $k_iV$ covering it. The sheaf axiom makes restriction $F[K]\to\prod_i\Gamma(k_iV,\mathcal O)$ injective. Each factor on the right is isomorphic as an $F$-vector space to the finite-dimensional $\Gamma(V,\mathcal O)$ of step 8. Consequently $F[K]$ is finite-dimensional. This proves finiteness without assuming that $K$ is reduced or smooth.

source.place: Lemma 23.10, p.487, finiteness refinement using the explicitly computed open kernel fibre; Jacobson and residue-field facts as stated in the cited nodes.

proof.text: For $k\in K(F)$ let $G_1$ act on $K$ by conjugation; normality makes this an action on $K$. The orbit theorem applies: $G_1$ is smooth connected affine of finite type and $K$ is separated of finite type. Its orbit is reduced and the orbit map factors through it as a scheme. A finite-dimensional algebra has finitely many prime ideals, all maximal; hence the underlying space of $K$ is finite discrete. The continuous image of connected $G_1$ is one point, namely $k$. The reduced orbit scheme is therefore $\operatorname{Spec}F$, using the closed-point residue-field theorem. Thus conjugation of $k$ is constant as a morphism, not only on $F$-points. In particular $k$ commutes with $T_1$ after every scalar extension, and the scheme-centralizer theorem gives $k\in T_1(F)$.

source.place: Finite-normal-kernel point argument supplementing Proposition 23.5 and Theorem 21.84; orbit theorem and maximal-torus self-centralizer.

proof.text: Every point of the finite scheme $K$ is a closed $F$-point and step 10 puts it in $T_1\subset C_1$. Therefore the open inverse image of $C_1$ in $K$ is the whole scheme $K$; an open immersion with the whole underlying open set is an isomorphism, regardless of nilpotents. Hence $K=K\cap C_1=V$ as schemes. The fibre calculation in step 8 is exactly the required kernel-coordinate isomorphism, with the prescribed embeddings $x_{1,\alpha}$. The subgroup intersection $T_1\cap U_{1,\alpha}=1$ was proved scheme-theoretically in step 2. When $q_\alpha=1$, $F[z]/(z)=F$, so that factor is the trivial scheme. When both root sets are empty, the regular-cocharacter theorem gives $G_i=T_i$; step 1 already proves all claims and the coordinate product is just $H$.
